speechtext:

subtopic: SCHEDULED HOCKEY GAMES BETWEEN SOVIET AND NHL TEAMS
SCHEDULED HOCKEY GAMES BETWEEN SOVIET AND NHL TEAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the midst of the spy embrouillage comes some good news in
Canadian-Soviet relations. It is announced that two top Soviet hockey teams, Central Red Army and Dynamo Riga, will play 14 team games against NHL teams during the next season. Games are scheduled with Vancouver, Edmonton, Calgary, and Quebec.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED SASKATCHEWAN DAM-EFFECT ON MANITOBA WATER RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, considerable concern has been expressed about the proposed Rafferty-Alameda dam project in Saskatchewan and the negative impact it will have on the environment of Saskatchewan and North Dakota. Virtually ignored in this debate is the impact this project will have on Manitoba.
The Souris River, which the Government of Saskatchewan proposes to dam, flows southward into North Dakota and then northward again into Manitoba. Damming the Souris River will have a negative impact on any jurisdiction downstream, including Manitoba. The quantity and quality of water flowing into Manitoba will be reduced and the leaching of heavy metals and mercury contamination could become a serious problem in that part of the Souris flowing into Manitoba.
The Rafferty-Alameda project is not a simple arrangement between Saskatchewan and North Dakota. The Souris River crosses the international boundary not once but twice, and the Rafferty-Alameda project will affect not one but two provincial jurisdictions. Despite this fact, no international treaty exists between all the parties affected, especially Manitoba. I call upon the Government to exercise its international responsibility on behalf of the people of Manitoba and refer this complex issue to the International Joint Commission for detailed consideration and negotiation.

June 29, 1988

subtopic: S.O. 21 ABORTION SUPREME COURT CASE-GOVERNMENT FUNDING SOUGHT BY WOMEN'S ORGANIZATIONS
S.O. 21 ABORTION SUPREME COURT CASE-GOVERNMENT FUNDING SOUGHT BY WOMEN'S ORGANIZATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as most Canadians know, Parliament is faced with the difficult challenge of rewriting Canada's abortion laws in light of the Supreme Court overturning Section 251 of the Criminal Code. There is also an important trial in the Supreme Court this fall, namely, the Joesph Borowski case, which would, in essence, give legal status and protection under the Charter to the unborn child.
The LEAF organization, which is the legal arm of the Advisory Council on the Status of Women, has applied for government funds to pay their legal fees because LEAF has interventionist status at the Borowski trial. This funding is in addition to what LEAF already gets from the Government currently. REAL women also have interventionist status, and are applying for government assistance as well.
I urge the Minister responsible for the status of women and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) to give funding to REAL women in fairness as the Government does not provide any funding to REAL women presently.
Under the Department's own guidelines, funding is not to go to any group involved with either side of the abortion issue. But in lieu of LEAF'S previous funding this stipulation obviously has been disregarded.

subsubtopic: EMPLOYMENT-REQUEST THAT JUSTICE BE PROVIDED FOR WOMEN OF KAHNAWAKE

"All they do is take money from the programs, it's always the same, they
take money and it's never enough."

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POSITION OF OPPOSITION PARTIES
CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POSITION OF OPPOSITION PARTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, history repeats itself. In the early forties, after trying in vain to interest central Canada and Europe, the Alberta Government accepted entrepreneurs from the United States who spent millions of dollars drilling dry holes before Leduc came in. That was the beginning of the oil industry in Alberta.
But you should have heard the Liberals and the CCF, now the NDP, rail about the Americans. "They will take over the country". "They will throw out our social programs", et cetera.
Today we are hearing the same predictions from the Liberals and the NDP about free trade. But none of the dire things happened. The Americans worked under Canadian rules, and we lost nothing. We gained an industry and millions of dollars worth of work and employment for hundreds of our people. The same good results can be secured from free trade. So free trade for a greater Canada!

subsubtopic: TREATMENT OF DEMONSTRATORS AT TORONTO ECONOMIC SUMMIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Sunday, June 19, over 140 demonstrators against the Summit Conference as a symbol of international greed and oppression committed civil disobedience. In a disciplined action they crossed over police barriers set up to block thousands of orderly protest marchers on University Avenue.
The police, after behaving very well in public, retaliated against those arrested afterwards by denying them their rights under Section 10(b) of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which states that everyone detained has a right to retain and instruct counsel without delay and to be informed of that right.
After several hours in jail the police refused to allow prisoners to phone lawyers, refused to allow lawyers to contact
June 29, 1988

or interview prisoners, and used systematic tricks and lies to deprive 140 people of their Charter right.
This deliberate and systematic violation of the Charter was planned in consultation with the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Kelleher), as he told us, who therefore shares responsibility for deliberate violation of the Charter.
I call on the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to apologize to Canadians for his Government's part in this violation of the Charter, and to order a public inquiry to determine who was responsible and what disciplinary action is needed to prevent a repetition of this grave government offence.

subsubtopic: UTILIZATION OF GREEN SPACES OF DOMAINE MAIZERETS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity today, and it is with great satisfaction that I rise in the House to emphasize the Government's commitment to environmental issues and heritage sites.

We must all work together, Mr. Speaker, to make every part of this country a good place to live.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-BUSINESS OPPORTUNITIES CONFERENCE
CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-BUSINESS OPPORTUNITIES CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday in my riding almost 400 people from small and medium-sized businesses attended one of those free trade business opportunities conferences much maligned by the Liberal and NDP Opposition.
They came to learn how to benefit from the free trade agreement, and they represent the reality of Canada in 1988, a Canada in which two-thirds of our exports are manufactured goods, a Canada that earns more export dollars from selling life insurance premiums abroad than from softwood lumber or crude oil, a Canada that earns more selling office equipment than from selling meat, a Canada in which sales of telecommunications equipment are four times the value of our nickel exports, a Canada where wheat exports are worth only half as much as our truck exports.

She said, "The Act isn't working and I felt I had to speak out".
In view of this harsh and unprecedented criticism of the Government, will the Minister of Justice now admit that his response to the unanimous report of the Justice Committee was a betrayal of the Prime Minister's 1984 promise to strengthen freedom of information, not to gut it? speechtext:

June 29, 1988

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture. Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the Hon. Member's question on this specific subject. I am quite aware of the position taken by certain farm leaders in the Province of Quebec which is, to a certain extent I suppose, shared by my provincial counterpart from that province.

I have seen the document that they have prepared. I have had senior people within my Department analyse it. It contains many inaccuracies and many flaws.

[ Translation]

Mr. Speaker, in this case, it is not an individual but a whole group of farmers' representatives, including the provincial Minister of Agriculture.

Mr. Speaker, I am rather surprised that the Hon. Member asks that question, particularly at this stage. He might recall that when we began the process of negotiating the bilateral trade arrangement between the United States and ourselves we made it very clear-it was publicly stated in this very Chamber, I believe on March 16, 1986-that Canada's supply managed systems, Canada's agri-food marketing systems, would remain intact. At the completion of the negotiations we delivered exactly what we stated on March 16, 1986.
In addition to that, there is a provision in the bilateral trade arrangement, Section 710 which clearly sets out that particular issue as part of the trade agreement. Canada's supply managed systems are quite consistent with the bilateral trade arrangement and are quite consistent with Article XI in the GATT.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Justice. Since 1977, only 1.6 per cent of women working in the Public Service have benefited from the federal pay equity law. A year ago this week, the Human Rights Commission recommended a major overhaul of the legislative provisions on pay equity.

subsubtopic: WAGE EQUITY-HUMAN RIGHTS COMMISSION RECOMMENDATIONS-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was this Government that introduced the Employment Equity Act. This Government introduced employment equity and broader affirmative action throughout the whole of the Public Service, and we will continue to bring equality into the Public Service in a way that had not been done in the past. We will do the same thing with Governor in Council appointments. We have done more in this field than any other Government.

Mr. Speaker, we know the legislation is not working. Why is the Government ignoring the proposals put forward by the Human Rights Commission? Why is it ignoring its commitment to pay equity for the women of Canada?

Mr. Speaker, the Employment Equity Act is working. The New Democrats did not want it to work in the first place, they argued against it. They voted against it. speechtext:

Recent testing for polyaromatic hydrocarbons in the Town of Newcastle, New Brunswick, has discovered samples which exceed the World Health Organization guidelines by at least tenfold. speakeroldname: Hon. Tom McMillan (Minister of the Environment):
subsubtopic: NEWCASTLE, N.B.-EFFECT OF POLYAROMATIC HYDROCARBONS ON WATER SUPPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Hon. Member will know, I have taken a very keen personal interest in this matter. The situation at Newcastle is serious. Polyaromatic hydrocarbons are an environmental bad actor. The Member will also know that the principal responsibility for this problem rests with the province and the municipality. However, for our part the federal Government is exercising its own jurisdiction to the hilt and backing the province and the community with all relevant and needed technical resources.
If the province or municipality need further assistance at any point in their own work, the Hon. Member can be assured I will instruct my officials to provide that assistance. In the meantime we are paying particular attention, because it is within federal jurisdiction, to water quality in the Miramachi River and to the marine life therein.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Although some Canadians will see a minor increase in their take-home pay this month, the Institute for Research and Public Policy confirms what we on this side of the House have being saying, that in fact middle-income Canadian families are worse off with so-called tax reform than they were in 1984. Mr. Speaker, many Members who have appeared before the committee have spoken to me not just about tax reform but about the tremendous growth we have had in this country and the fact we are leading the G-7 countries in job creation and economic growth, the fact that we have seen 1.3 million jobs created during this period of time, and the fact that we are taking the courageous move to reform the tax system. As the Hon. Member has pointed out, that will become evident to Canadians in their first pay cheque after July 1. I believe 85 per cent of Canadians will see their taxes go down.
These are the things Canadians are interested in. These are the things I am hearing from people when they come and congratulate me on the performance we have seen by this Government and by this economy over the last three and one-half years.

The Minister takes $22 billion out of the pockets of Canadians, returns $2 billion and thinks they should be grateful.
Will the Minister confirm that although some of these tax decreases are effective since January, the payroll deductions only become effective in July and, therefore, the Government has been enjoying an interest-free loan of $1 billion from taxpayers?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT

speechtext:
The House resumed from Tuesday, June 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. Crosbie that Bill C-130, an Act to implement the Free Trade Agreement between Canada and the United States of America, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee, and the amendment of Mr. Axworthy:
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "That" and substituting the following therefor:
"this House opposes in principle and therefore declines to proceed with Bill C-130, an Act to implement the Free Trade Agreement between Canada and the United States of America, because that agreement, which was negotiated

June 29, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
in a secretive and irresponsible manner in the absence of a mandate from the Canadian people, will undermine the economic, social and political institutions of Canada, because it will fail to provide guaranteed and secure access to U.S. and other world trade markets, because it will create severe adverse effects on many industries and communities and because it will endanger the economic and social fabric and political independence of Canada."
And the amendment of Mr. Langdon:
That the amendment be amended by adding immediately after the words ''political institutions of Canada," the words "including our valued system of social and regional development programs,".

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are here today to discuss one of the most devastating pieces of legislation ever brought before the House of Commons. We are here to debate a Bill which will finish Canada as we know it and replace it with a Canada that will become nothing more than a colony of the United States.
So urgent and compelling is the impatience of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to pack up this country and ship it south that we are going to debate this Bill for only a few hours. It took 121 years for Canadians to build this Confederation. The Government is proposing to undo that in less than half that number of hours. This Bill represents over 1,000 days of intricate negotiations between the two countries. We will debate the result of those 1,000 days in five days before the House of Commons.

This Bill is a disaster like the trade agreement it will give force of law.
With this measure, the Government is telling Canadians they have no choice but to accept or reject this agreement. It is telling this House that the elected representatives of the Canadian people have no say in the drafting of this Bill and can do nothing to diminish its impact on our country.
We are being forced to pass this legislation in a matter of days without even having seen the corresponding U.S. bill.
At every stage of the talks, there were major differences of opinion between both governments about the wording and the content of the agreement. Nevertheless, this Government is now obliging us to adopt its version of the Bill without giving us a chance to examine the legislation proposed in the U.S. Congress.
Only two and a half weeks ago, the Prime Minister's Chief of Staff was still in Washington to negotiate differences between the United States and Canada, not just on minor points but on fundamental issues like the definition of subsidies.

This Bill greatly offends Canadian tradition in three ways: it is anti-parliamentary, it is anti-democratic, it is anti-Constitution. We are being presented with an omnibus Bill which changes 27 existing Acts of Parliament. Clause 8 commits us never again to pass a statute inconsistent with this Bill, never again to enact legislation inconsistent with this trade deal. The
Bill is to supersede any other Act of Parliament, past or future. It has almost the authority of a constitutional provision. Yet the discussion draft that the U.S. Congress negotiated between the U.S. Senate and the House of Representatives indicates that that version of the trade Bill, the American version of the trade Bill, can be amended by any subsequent Act of Congress. Not only that, we find that Canadians can be fined, even imprisoned, for contravening American law, present and future, laws we haven't even seen yet.
I raised this in the House of Commons. The Minister was surprised. Now we know why. He has not read the whole deal. He has not studied the document. I am going to take him and the House through several of the provisions that relate right to the fundamental nature of our country. I doubt that the government Members read any of the Bill at all. Here is what it says about people who do not uphold the trade agreement as incorporated into the Bill.
Section 77.26 (1)-Every person who contravenes or fails to comply with ... (C) a protective order covering business proprietary and other privileged information made under American law ... is guilty of offence and is liable ... (E) on conviction and indictment, to a fine not exceeding one million dollars.
The Bill before this House involves Canadians in potential liability, potential imprisonment, and fines up to $1 million, not for offending Canadian law, not for contravening Canadian regulation, but for offending American law, present or future, laws that have not yet been enacted by the U.S. Congress. The Bill is anti-parliamentary for those reasons, and it is also anti-democratic.
Turning to public hearings, we do not know whether the committee will allow public hearings. There have been no public hearings on this Bill to date. There were no public hearings allowed on the text of the agreement. The only hearings across the country were on the general principles of that agreement. There has been no opportunity for Canadians publicly, before their elected representatives or Members of Parliament, to analyse the deal, to make their points, their submissions, to present their briefs on the deal, to analyse the real impact of the deal on their lives, their unions, their jobs, their professions, their businesses.
The whole procedure has been anti-democratic. The Prime Minister has no mandate for this legislation. It alters the fundamental direction of Canada. There was no mention of it in the last general election. It was not a theme put before the people of Canada in the last election. The only time Canadians were ever given an inkling, given an understanding of the Prime Minister's view on this very fundamental issue was when he sought the leadership of the Conservative Party at its national convention in 1983, and when, in response to a debate with the current Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), the current Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie), the current Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), he was asked what he thought about free trade and his words were
June 29, 1988

quite clear. "Free trade," he said, "it affects our sovereignty, and we will have none of it."
Those were the words of the Prime Minister when it suited him to be against free trade. Our Prime Minister's aversion to sticking to his word has become famous. Some would say even legendary.
Canadians were not consulted nor did they authorize a deal which changes the whole direction of Canadian history, and we need an election so that Canadians can decide.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this Bill is not only anti-parliamentary and anti-democratic, it is antiConstitution.
Clause 6-the Minister hasn't read it, he doesn't know, people ask him questions and he's taken by surprise-Clause 6 contains a provision that allows the federal Government to ignore the jurisdiction of the provinces in order to implement the agreement. This would involve not just wine and grapes, as was claimed by the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) but also energy, agriculture, our financial institutions, social policies, services, culture, and so forth. In other words, the present Government has allowed the Americans to rewrite our Constitution and to determine our future legislative agenda.

You must be asking yourself the question, Mr. Speaker: How did it come to this? Why? Why are we being forced to rush this Bill through at the last minute, against all our traditions, parliamentary, democratic, constitutional, against the wishes of a vast majority of the Canadian people who want an election before this deal is implemented?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Why? Why are we now
being forced to give hasty approval to legislation which represents the largest sell-out of our sovereignty since we became a nation in 1867? Why? Dishonesty, Mr. Speaker, dishonesty on the part of this Government.
The whole point of getting into bilateral negotiations with the United States rather than negotiating with that country internationally as we have done since the War quite successfully, the sole point of getting into bilateral negotiations was to obtain secure access to the American market. Secure access to the American market meant a specific exemption from U.S. protectionist trade remedy law. It also meant an impartial binding dispute settlement mechanism to enforce that exemption.
We in this Party have been saying that ever since these negotiations first started. I put it in questions to the Prime Minister; my colleague from Winnipeg-Fort Garry put it in questions to the Minister for International Trade. I told the
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
Ottawa Board of Trade in a major speech two years ago this month that any agreement with the United States that did not have a specific exemption from American trade law, that did not exempt us from protectionist legislation-the 1930 Trade Act of the United States, the 1974 trade law of the United States, the current omnibus Bill still being discussed in the Congress-that any agreement with the United States that did not give us that exemption, that did not give us a binding dispute settlement mechanism, was not worth the paper it was written on.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
The Government, the Prime Minister, his Ministers, used to agree with me on that point.
A year ago the Prime Minister said in New York, quoted by the Wall Street Journal in response to some American reporters: "The U.S. trade remedy laws cannot apply to Canada period". That was when he understood the deal. The former Minister for International Trade, the Hon. Member for Vancouver Centre (Miss Carney), said that the objective of any trade agreement-and she said this in the House of Commons-would be the elimination of countervail by both countries. The current Minister for International Trade agreed with his predecessor and with the Prime Minister. Here is what he said in St. John's, on July 2, 1987, a year ago, before the St. John's Board of Trade, and I use the Minister's words:
Unless we get out from under the threat of countervail and other U.S. trade remedy law and unless there is an effective dispute settlement resolution to bind the Americans to their commitments, a free trade agreement with the United States would not be a good deal for Canada.
Those were the Minister's words. We have been saying that ever since these negotiations started. We have been attempting to hold the Government to that sole purpose of any bilateral negotiation with the United States. Well, we all know that the Minister for International Trade is trying to bluff his way through, trying to sell this arrangement to Canadians with jokes and anecdotes. Perhaps that speech in St. John's was one of them, but then again the Minister has not read the deal. He is the man who compares selling this trade agreement to the United States with selling vacuum cleaners. For his information-and I feel I owe him now the responsibility of taking him through the deal that he has not read-this is what the deal says in the actual text. The Minister will have great difficulty comparing that with his last July statement to the St. John's Board of Trade. Article 1902:1 of this trade deal says that the United States:
-reserves the right to apply its anti-dumping law and countervailing duty law to goods imported from the territory of the other Party.
The other party is Canada. In other words, there is no exemption from U.S. protectionist trade law. It is the same law that crippled us on exports of softwood lumber, fish, potash, and put on quotas against steel. Those laws still apply.

June 29, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
Yes, it is true, we will have a new trade tribunal, but how will this trade tribunal ensure our exports guaranteed access to the American market? How will it protect our exporters from that protectionist American legislation? Well, the Prime Minister cannot tell us. We put the question to him. The Minister cannot tell us because he has not read it. The reason the Government cannot tell us is that the trade tribunal will not protect us or give us an exemption from American trade law. Not only will the procedure be longer and costlier for our exporters, the tribunal still will not be able to challenge U.S. law.
Here again I turn to the agreement. How can the Minister know? He has not read the whole deal. But Article 1904:2 states that the tribunal can review a trade decision of the United States Government only:
-to determine whether such determination was in accordance with the antidumping or countervailing duty law of the importing Party.
That is American law. It goes on to say that:
-the anti-dumping and countervailing duty statutes of the Parties, as those statutes may be amended from time to time, are incorporated into this Agreement.
In other words, the tribunal cannot challenge the law. Canadian exporters will not be able to challenge American law. The tribunal has the jurisdiction only to interpret that law using American precedent and American judicial practice. Nothing has changed for Canadian exporters. If an American industry feels that a Canadian industry by way of export into the American market is obtaining a share of that market which the Americans cannot tolerate, they have the same remedies in countervail, in quotas, in anti-dumping, and in surtax as they had before this agreement was ever signed.
Canadian exporters are being invited into the Prime Minister's brave new world of trade, with the United States, under the same rules. Not only existing American rules, but as the article I have just recited says, under any American statute present or future as they may be amended from time to time- present American law, future American law, and no restriction on the sovereign authority of the United States.
Also, even at this late date we do not know whether the tribunal's decisions will be considered constitutional by the American courts. Our Ambassador to the United States was properly concerned. He is quoted as saying the following in what seems to me to be the understatement of the year. These were his words:
We would be profoundly concerned if the net result of the U.S. legal constraints is that panel decisions-
That is to say, decisions of the tribunal:
-cannot be implemented under U.S. law.

This House is being forced to pass this proposed legislation at top speed, when we don't even know if the U.S. Government
will have to abide by the tribunal's decisions or whether it will be able to act on those decisions.
Mr. Speaker, I always thought that in business, when one party enters into an agreement with another party and the latter cannot meet his commitments, the agreement is automatically cancelled. Apparently that is not how this Government sees it. Otherwise, we would not be here to rush through approval of our part of an agreement while the other party is not even sure it will be able to abide by its provisions.

What is completely incomprehensible, Mr. Speaker, and totally unacceptable is that despite the fact the Government opposite by its own admission did not get what it wanted in this deal from the Americans, namely, secure access to the U.S. market, an exemption from American protectionist trade law, it went ahead, continued the negotiations, and concluded the negotiations despite its failure to meet that objective.
The principal condition for a deal with the United States was not met by the Americans. Their markets will remain as protectionist and as protected as ever. Their lumber industry will continue to use protectionist trade remedy laws whenever it feels threatened, as will their steel industry, as will their potash industry, as will their fishing industry, as will their textile industry, as will their agricultural industry, because the Government opposite, led by the Prime Minister, did not have the guts to stand up and say to the Americans: "Give us the purpose for which we entered these negotiations. Give us secure access to your market. Give us a guarantee against harassment, a guarantee against unilateral trade law or else there is no deal".

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Why? Because this Government did not have the courage or the honesty to return to the people of Canada with a failed initiative. This Prime Minister did not have the courage or the honesty to say to the people of our country, "Well, we tried, but we failed". The Prime Minister had too much political capital invested in getting a deal, any deal, on any terms.
There are those who tell us that Canada need not worry about losing its national personality. Some of us sat in this House listening to the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom assure us that there was nothing to worry about in this trade deal. She pointed to the experience of the European Economic Community. She told us that Britain, France, Germany, and the other nations have kept their distinctive nationalities although they are part of the European Community.
That completely ignores a simple reality. This is not Europe. This is not a case of several countries with a distinctive history of 1,000 years, with distinctive languages, of relatively equal size, trading together for a common purpose. On this continent, Canada is roughly one-tenth the power, the size, and the population of the United States. On this continent, we have only half of Europe's history. On this continent, the sole reason
June 29, 1988

for most of us living here is that we wanted a distinct personality, we wanted a nation north of the 49th parallel. We wanted to be Canadian.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
We are concerned, Mr. Speaker, about maintaining our national personality. We are concerned with maintaining our national integrity, our cultural identity, control over our resources, our economy, our social programs, and our regional development programs-no north and south division as in the United Kingdom. Ours is a country where there is equality of opportunity from the Atlantic to the Pacific to the northern Arctic. We are concerned over our ability to set an independent foreign policy. These are the issues at stake.
Mr. Speaker, from the very beginning of these talks, the Government tried to convince us that we were examining a free trade agreement. That is a myth that should be laid to rest once and for all. In spite of its title and the Government's definitions, this agreement is not free trade.
I also think we should avoid getting into the debate about whether we are for or against the philosophy of free trade, we in the Liberal Party have always been in favour of freer trade, of liberalizing trade and reducing tariff barriers. What we are discussing today is not free trade. It is a selective trade agreement. A number of industries are included and a number are excluded. We must analyse the FTA like any other contract. What did we gain and what did we lose? What did we get and what did we give away?
But read it! Whatever I go in Canada, I tell Canadians: Read the text. And now I have to say the same thing to the Minister: Read the document, sir.
This is not free trade. And it is an agreement that is costing us a pretty penny. We are paying the price every day ...

If it were just a matter of lowering trade barriers, lowering tariffs, we as a Party have always been in favour of that, always in favour of broadening our commerce. We have to remind the House and the country that 80 per cent of all the transactions that now move across the Canadian-American border either way go forward free of tariff. We succeeded under successive Liberal administrations since the War in achieving that. All we are talking about is the remaining 20 per cent, and for that remaining 20 per cent, this Prime Minister gave away the store.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Shame.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
We have yielded control over investment. The limit for review of direct takeovers has been raised to $ 150 million. Any company worth less than that
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
can be bought up by the Americans and no one in Canada will have anything to say about it. In the case of indirect takeovers, there will be no limit at all. It will be takeovers unlimited.
Just in case there was any doubt that the Americans are being invited to buy up our own country, this legislation turns 242 million Americans into Canadians for the purposes of the Investment Canada Act. How could the Minister know that? He has not read the deal.
Clause 14.1 (10)(a) says:
Every reference in those provisions to "Canadian" shall be read and
construed as a reference to "American" and every reference in those provisions
to "non-Canadian" shall be read and construed as a reference to "nonCanadian other than American".
The Government says that this new investment will bring jobs and prosperity. We have not seen any valid projections that demonstrate that. Ninety-four per cent of all foreign investment in this country since this Government took power in 1984 has been takeovers of existing companies, not new investment, not new jobs. Where are the new jobs that have flowed from these takeovers in the last four years?

Mr. Speaker, we have given up control over our capital markets. What does this Bill say about our banking system? The Bank Act is amended. From now on, Americans will no longer be non-residents of Canada under Section 109.1. Five Americans or five unrelated U.S. corporations will be able to own and operate an American bank in Canada and even buy a Canadian chartered bank. I am not going to allow this Government to rewrite history. It has been Liberal Governments, working through international negotiations, that brought tariffs down from an average of 40 per cent at the end of the last war to 4 per cent today. Liberal Governments brought our tariff structure to the United States to a point where, as I said earlier, 80 per cent of everything that moves across our mutual border, either way, is free of the impost of customs and tariff. We achieved that without giving away our sovereignty. All we are talking about in improving our trading relationship with the United States is the remaining 20 per cent. For that, the Prime Minister gave away the store.
The Liberal Party has always favoured, and still favours, more liberalized trade, not only with the United States but with all our trading partners. Under the Government opposite, our trade with the Pacific Rim and with Europe has deteriorated badly. As we outlined in our report entitled "Expanding Choices-The Liberal Alternative to the Mulroney Trade Deal", which I had the honour of presenting with my colleague, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry, we believe that as essential, vital and crucial as the American market is to us, we have always done better in negotiating with the United States under the umbrella of international negotiations rather than taking on the strongest economic power in the world head-to-head bilaterally.
We have always done better internationally than by attempting to deal bilaterally and exclusively with the United States, particularly when a Government of Canada appears to want the deal so much more than the Americans.
We would continue to pursue sectoral opportunities like the Auto Pact. We would look for ways to eliminate those irritants to trade. Yes, we believe this country needs a more vigorous trading policy, but a Liberal trading policy would allow us to trade with the world, with special emphasis on the United States, not just an exclusive deal with the United States.

With a Liberal trade strategy the first step would be to eliminate interprovincial barriers. We should begin by experimenting with free trade in Canada. We would introduce a bill which would clearly spell out our trade objectives, financing methods and trade remedy mechanism. We would also regroup within a single administration the talents of our trade experts, in order to concentrate the federal Government's efforts on an essential objective, which is to develop our foreign markets to create permanent jobs for Canadians.
No trade policy can replace a national economic strategy. Rather, a trade policy ought to be part and parcel of such a strategy. No trade agreement, either with the United States, Europe or Japan could make us more skilled or competitive. We must do that ourselves. We must increase research and development investments. We are not going to ensure economic growth by applying technology developed by others.

We need to develop our education system and give our young people the skills they need for the jobs of tomorrow. We will commit ourselves to a full employment strategy, to supplementation for the working poor, to better training and retraining for our workforce, to a national literacy program and to a national apprenticeship program. When I have the responsibility to go to Washington to talk to the Americans, whether it be about trade, employment, acid rain, the fishery or about the Arctic, our Arctic, I will not start with the assumption that getting their co-operation means surrendering our political independence and surrendering our sovereignty. That surrender has been the result of this Government's strategy and we can see the results of that approach in this trade deal.
We who oppose this deal are painted by the Prime Minister as being afraid or timid, of having no confidence in our future and no confidence in Canada. That Prime Minister is dead wrong. We do have confidence in this country. We do have confidence in Canada. We do have confidence in our future. The difference is that for us our future is not a continental future. Our future is a Canadian future.
On the trade issue, I am not saying we can do it alone. What I am saying is that we can do it in our own way. We have proved for over 120 years that we can resist that north-south pull of continental forces. We have proved we can create and
June 29, 1988

build a flourishing, proud and self-sufficient nation. I have full confidence in this country and full confidence in our fellow citizens. I believe we are now mature enough, talented enough, confident enough and tough enough to build our own future in our own way by making our own decisions.
In 1867, the Fathers of Confederation established this House of Commons and the other place. They gave this Chamber the responsibility to build a great sovereign independent nation. They gave our predecessors the responsibility of establishing a unique and distinct nation on the northern half of our continent. If this legislation is allowed to pass, it will be said that in 1988 this House abdicated that role set for us by the founders of our country, that we surrendered that responsibility and abandoned our sovereignty. As a nation, we cannot allow that to happen.
The Minister scoffs, the Prime Minister sloughs it off, but this debate is really about the future of Canada as an independent and sovereign nation. It is about our ability to maintain that sovereignty. It is about our ability to govern our own country, for our own people, in our own way. It is for us to make our own political decisions as to how we want to determine our own economy, our own social programs, our own culture and protect our regions. It is for us to define, establish, maintain and promote our own values and our own national purpose.

Mr. Speaker, I look forward to making a few comments on this very important topic of free trade. I would like to begin by putting this debate and my comments in the context of some of the current trade statistics.
One-third of Canada's GNP comes from export. Compare that to Japan which is 20 per cent, or the United States which is 10 per cent. Close to three million Canadians jobs are directly related to export and 80 per cent of our exports go to
June 29, 1988
the United States. Close to 2.25 million jobs are directly related to exports to the United States.
The Canada-United States trade is the largest in the world. The Ontario-United States trade is larger than that of the United States and of Japan. Ninety per cent of the exports from Ontario go to the United States. Just to put this in an historic context, in 1946, 40 per cent of our exports went to the United States. In 1988, 80 per cent of our exports go to the United States. In other words, our exports have doubled.
These statistics are very important for us to keep in mind when dealing with a free trade debate. We are not starting at zero, we are starting with a very high level of trade with the United States. We also have a high level of free trade with the United States as a result of the Tokyo Round from 1979 to 1987. As of January 1, 1988, 80 per cent of our exports to the United States went tariff-free and 65 per cent of their exports came into Canada tariff-free.
The Government's motivations in this free trade initiative are very important and can be summarized under three headings. First, it is our purpose to secure that high level of trade that we have with the United States now. We wish to secure that high level against the growing protectionism within the United States.
Our second objective is to bring a dispute resolution mechanism to solve trade disputes between our two nations. For example, in the last few years, there have been fishing disputes, disputes dealing with the shakes and shingles industry and disputes dealing with potash, just to name three.
Our third major objective is to enhance that trade. As I said, the motivations of the Government are first to secure the high level of trade we have with the United States, second to bring in a dispute resolution mechanism and third to enhance that trade and to create jobs.
This is trade with the richest market on earth, living right next door to us. Surely any other nation in the world would give its eye-teeth for the opportunity that we have at this time. That is what we have seized-

The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner), earlier this afternoon, said that we had no mandate to conclude

this free trade agreement. I would suggest that we have a very clear mandate to create jobs. I think everyone on all sides of the House would accept that. Surely then our record in job creation is second to none. Not only are we supposed to create jobs, but we should protect the jobs we already have. That is the one thing that this trade agreement seeks to do. First it seeks to protect and to secure what we have and then to enhance that.
I would suggest that we are seeking to secure the high level of trade and the relationship that we have now, second to none other in the world, and surely we have a mandate to do that against the growing protectionism in the United States. Therefore, I would submit to those in the Opposition who say that we have no mandate that they think again.
What does this free trade agreement do? It does three simple things. First, it eliminates all barriers to trade in goods and services between Canada and the United States. It does that in three ways. Some are eliminated immediately on January 1, 1989. Others are eliminated in five equal steps over the next five years. The remainder are to be eliminated in 10 equal steps over the next 10 years. Second, the free trade agreement significantly expands and frees the conditions of cross-border investment. Third, it establishes procedures for joint administration and for a dispute resolution mechanism.
It is also important to realize what the trade agreement does not do. It does not permit the free exchange of labour which is similar to what occurs in the Common Market. It merely provides for temporary passes for those who service equipment. Second, it does not affect Canada's regional development programs, pension programs, medicare programs, child care initiatives, welfare programs, unemployment insurance programs, education programs, pornography control, gun control or ownership and regulation of resources. Those all remain in our hands. Third, it does not create a customs union like the Common Market. Both Canada and the United States will still have their own external trade policies. Fourth, it is not an economic union with a common Parliament as is the case in Europe. It is really just a trade agreement.
As I listened to Liberal and NDP comments made in the House and to comments made by other Liberal leftist commentators, with all their whining, complaining and misleading statements about the free trade agreement, I found that their comments appeared to me to be similar to the techniques employed by Joseph Goebbels. The technique he used was that if you say something loud enough, if you say it long enough and if you repeat it over and over, then it becomes true. I think the tactics used by some of those in this debate are nothing short of shameful. I am struck by the fact that-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1984 the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said:
Canadians rejected free trade in 1911. They would do so again-
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) said:
Bilateral free trade with the United States is simplistic and naive. It would
only serve to further diminish our ability to compete internationally.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) said:
Free trade ... raises the possibility that thousands of jobs could be lost...
Before we jump on the band-wagon of continentalism, we should strengthen
our industrial structure so that we are more competitive.
They were right then, and they are wrong now to force this agreement on Canadians.
I have said in previous speeches that this trade deal entrenches U.S. protectionism, especially dealing with lumber and fish. It fails to give access to key U.S. markets. It gives unwarranted concessions to U.S. demands and subjects us to U.S. law. It gives the U.S. guaranteed access to Canadian resources, and many feel this includes water. It undermines Canadian energy prices, preventing economic diversification in the West. It opens the door for more U.S. takeovers of Canadian industries. It will destroy key agricultural sectors of our economy. There will be a loss of well-paid union jobs, and women in service industries will be victimized. Regional development programs may very well be at risk when they are considered unfair subsidies.
Today I want to concentrate on the impact of the deal on social programs and health policies. As we all know, Canadians are very proud of our social programs which far exceed those in the U.S. in providing for Old Age Security, protecting the unemployed, assisting families with young children, and providing free medicare for all our citizens. We believe these are inviolable social rights in Canada.
Despite government attempts to deny it, experts agree that this trade deal will have both direct and indirect effects on health and social programs. The Government maintains the public welfare is protected, yet ignores the fact that the U.S. explicitly targeted unemployment insurance as a "government-created trade distortion" in the Atlantic groundfish countervailing duty case. This undoubtedly was a precedent and should have been a warning to the Government. If, as the Government claims, social programs are exempted and not to be threatened by this deal, why did it not ensure this by including a specific clause to this effect?
Article 1907 leaves it wide open for subsidies to be defined over the next seven years through a process of negotiation. There is no guarantee that the Americans will not target any
of our social programs as unfair subsidies under U.S. trade law. In fact, U.S. businesses have always considered that medicare, unemployment and regional development programs are unfair subsidies. Why did the Canadian Government not insist on a specific clause exempting social programs, similar to the cultural industries exemption in Article 2005? This could have been done.
Already the Government is adopting American-style practices in the field of social programs. There are many examples of Government encouraging increased privatization of services, by the Minister condoning provincial practices contrary to the Canada Health Act, and by encouraging commercialization of child care and services for the elderly.
Annex 1408 of the chapter on services in the agreement lists management services covered by this deal. It specifically lists management of general hospitals, psychiatric and children's hospitals, community health clinics, and others. This means that U.S. firms can take over management of such facilities in Canada and operate them for profit as is common practice in the U.S. We already see a trend in this direction in Ontario.
Studies show that standards suffer when services are privatized. Staff are cut and qualifications are not as high. Profits are the primary goal. Our system of medicare is much better and also much cheaper than the American system. Our system costs 30 per cent less than the American system and operates with 13 per cent less staff. U.S. privatized hospitals charge 22 per cent more on average for patient admission than we do in Canada. Do we want an Americanized system of medicare where 35 million people have no coverage at all and where the cost of an illness can bankrupt a family? Of course not.
It is bad enough that the Government is encouraging privatization with poor quality care in Canada, but it is extremely serious that this deal will allow U.S. companies to participate on an equal footing in Canada and enshrines these rights in an international trade deal.
Another very serious section affecting social programs is a giveaway section on monopolies buried in Chapter 20. This requires Canadians to consult with Americans before creating a monopoly, a term which could apply to all our universal social programs. Under this part Canada will lose the ability to create accessible, affordable programs for all Canadians. This could seriously affect future planning of social programs.
Under this agreement the Prime Minister can overrule provincial jurisdiction in health and welfare in the interests of establishing a level-playing field. U.S. child care chains, operating with minimum standards, will have open access to Canadian communities, with the right of public funding. American service firms are given the right to acquire businesses here and the right to national treatment. Disagreement on this matter will be settled through the dispute settlements mechanism. However, this process will undoubtedly influence Canadian policies in the future. It will require us to conform more with inferior U.S. practices.
June 29, 1988

Canadians do not want a Kentucky Fried Chicken type of child care. We want quality care for our kids, care that is affordable and not run just for profit. This agreement will have a very significant impact on the social contract that Canadians hold dear. The policy of harmonization, the level-playing field concept, will force Canadian firms to conform to the pressure of very powerful U.S. market forces. Workers will be affected, their wages and working conditions will be influenced by lower U.S. standards. Fewer workers will be unionized. Women will be forced into lower paid part-time jobs. Family benefits like the Family Allowance and child tax credit will be frowned upon and eroded as unfair subsidies.
Canadians have different expectations than Americans. We have fought hard, led by CCF pioneers, to establish comprehensive universal social programs like old age pensions, family allowances, unemployment insurance and medicare. We pay for these through our taxes. We try to redistribute incomes in a much fairer way to eliminate poverty. This is not the U.S. way. Canada is different than the U.S. We want to remain that way. We do not want to be sold off by a Tory Government through this agreement to become the fifty-first state.
The Prime Minister had no mandate to negotiate and impose this deal on Canadians. He had an obligation to call an election and go to the people with the real truth about the dangers of this deal for Canada and Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, may I say that this is the most rewarding opportunity I have had since my election to the House of Commons, an opportunity to speak to the issue which I consider to be the most significant for Canadians and young people, in short for our whole economy: garanteed access to the United States market.
Before dealing specifically with the matter I should like to go over some of the remarks made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) when he delivered his speech on free trade earlier this afternoon. For instance he accused us and said that we would tear up or spend only five days debating the free trade issue while it took 120 years just to get prepared for that United States market. I might respond by saying that he wants to take half a second to tear up what Canadians took 120 years to achieve. While he is telling us that he did not have time and that we do not have enough time to study free trade, I would remind him that he should have read the report of and listened to the committee of the House of Commons which has heard many representations from Canadians here in Ottawa and in other major cities. Among others, he should also have listened to the Conseil du patronat, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the Economic Council of Canada, and the Canadian Federation of Independent Business. He should read the reports of those organizations and listen to what they have to say.
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
He should also have heard and read the evidence before the Quebec National Assembly, before a parliamentary commission where Quebecers made representations on free trade, a parliamentary commission made up of MNAs from both sides, Liberals and Pequistes. He should also have read and listened to the remarks of Quebec Liberal Premier Bourassa. He should have listened to the leader of the Opposition, Mr. Parizeau, to former Parti Quebecois Minister Landry and to Mr. MacDonald, the Liberal minister. Lastly, instead of saying that Canadians will not have time to study the free trade deal, he should have told the Canadian public that a committee made up of Members of this House will also hear representations from Canadians. We will probably be told before this committee that free trade means opportunities for Canadian products.
You will know that Canadians now produce some $500 billion worth of goods and services. A quarter of that or $125 billion is exported. And that quarter, Mr. Speaker, accounts for 3 million jobs for Canadians and of those $125 billion, 80 percent or $95 billion are exports to the United States. And that is what the Liberal Party and the socialists object to! I am both pleased and saddened to lump them together, but I can only say that they are the ones who lumped themselves together in a coalition. That is the $95 billion market that the Leader of the Liberal Party would have torn up. What does that $95 billion means for Quebec? It means in comparative terms that where Canadian production stands at $500 billion, Quebec production stands at $100 billion and that out of Canadian exports totalling $125 billion, Quebec exports $20 billion. That $20 billion accounts for 800 000 jobs for Quebec men and women and out of that $20 billion, 76 percent is exported to the United States, that is to say $16 billion worth of goods and services from Quebec. That means wood, electricity, manufactured goods, furniture, metal products, aircraft, aircraft engines, and so on and the 650 000 jobs that Quebeckers owe to the American market that they would take away from us.
And for those who do not know Quebec's history, Mr. Speaker, that market is very important because in Quebec, since 1960, there has been a lot of fast changes. In 1960, under a Liberal Government that had a different kind of policies than Liberals here, we went through the "Quiet Revolution". The Quiet Revolution meant that in our universities we got rid of the staple training of doctors, lawyers and priests. Instead, we trained business people, engineers, scientists, etc. We also had the "Masters in our own House" policy under which Quebecers increasingly assumed control of their own economy. We now need a market. And recently the Quebec Government, under both the Parti quebecois and the Liberals, put in place systems to promote new financing structures for our business corporations. In other words, it favoured equity investments in our corporations. Those corporations are now ready to go, thanks to the Registered Share Purchasing Funds, thanks to the Caisse de depot.

Those corporations now have the capital needed. The Quiet Revolution also gave them the brainpower needed, the young educated professionals.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, 14 per cent of our business leaders and top executives in Quebec are under 30 years of age.
This is what we want for Quebecers, and this is why I support free trade. This is also why I blame the Liberals for not supporting free trade, because those young Quebecers have the education and the capital needed, they are all set and ready to go, and in Quebec we want to sell on the American market, and we have no wish of the Americans putting up tariff barriers again, as we saw in the case of softwood lumber, and as we are now seeing in the case of pork carcasses.
Mr. Speaker, why do Liberals want to scrap the deal? Why are they suggesting to Canadian business people: "You erred, you were wrong in selling to the United States, you should have sold elsewhere-in Europe, in Asia"?
Canadian business people get into the nearest market the same way someone who launches a business does in his village, in his town, in his region-at first he sells to the market next door.
And when I heard today the Leader of the Liberal Party (Mr. Turner) suggest: "We should overlook the American market, the market that has the money, the market that buys our products, the market that knows our products, the market that has a compatible economy with our own in terms of consumer habits and production" ... If were to believe the Liberals, we should overlook that market, go to Europe, go around the world, go to Asia.
Have you ever seen business people forget about their regular customers and say: "We will go 3000 miles farther to sell our goods." That is nonsense, Mr. Speaker, and that is what the Liberals want us to do.
To me, that way of thinking seems to be obstructing Quebec's growth, and I find it very strange that the Liberal Premier of Ontario (Mr. Peterson) had allied himself with the Liberal caucus here, and has approved the statements made by the Liberal leader. The objective of that alliance is to harm Quebec. That alliance, and that is where the Liberals agree in fact with the Socialists, is to the advantage of southern Ontario.
Because, you see, the riding with 740 000 workers who have benefitted from a free trade deal since 1965 is in fact the one represented by the leader of the Socialist Party (M. Broad-bent), the Oshawa riding. We all know about the free trade deal negotiated in 1965, which is working and which guarantees $30 billions in exports of Canadian made end products. Mr. Speaker, $30 billions are ensured by a free trade deal in southern Ontario, and the Liberals are joined in a coalition. They want all Canadians to be denied the benefits and the "profitability" of free trade in southern Ontario. And that is why the workers from southern Ontario are literally ripped off, because they pay union dues not to finance their collective
bargaining sessions, but to finance the harsh campaign the Socialist party has now launched against free trade.
Mr. Speaker, I will conclude by saying that it is important for us to vote for free trade because it is important that between January 1, 1989 and the following 10 years tariff rates fall to zero. It is important that our possible disputes be settled in an orderly manner by a binational tribunal. And that is provided in the agreement, a dispute settlement mechanism, some court that will protect us from any negative action by American protectionism.
So Canadians will surely understand, something I doubt the coalition can do, but we will campaign on that issue, and the Canadian people will give us a mandate to sell it to the United States in order that our businesses keep on flourishing.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. The Hon. Member says the Prime Minister did not try to cut back senior citizens' pensions. There are thousands of seniors in my riding who will attest to the fact that he tried to cut back pensions. Since it took office, the Government has had a hidden agenda to cut back universality, cut back on family allowances and cut back on senior citizens' pensions.
We watched Conservative back-benchers and the bookends clap and wave when Prime Minister Thatcher tried to tell us how to develop our social programs in this country. I do not want to have the rich and poor, the have and have-not Thatcherite philosophy as the philosophy for this country. We have been bamboozled and scamboozled by a Government that is not interested in the best interests of Canadians, but more interested in trying to save the Prime Minister's political hide.
The Prime Minister was acting from a position of desperation. On the Thursday night, Simon Reisman, the chief negotiator, said there was no deal. What happened between Thursday and Sunday? What miracle portended so that suddenly Canadians who had walked away from the table saying it was over now said it would go forward? It was the sale of Canada through our energy policies. It was the continental energy policy, the Achilles heel, for which the United States has waited for generations.
Between Thursday and Sunday Canadians said: "If you do not want to sign the deal, we will give you national treatment for energy". All renewable and non-renewable energy in Canada, including water, is included in the deal. In times of energy shortage every renewable and non-renewable resource, including natural gas, must be sold to the Americans in a proportion determined by this agreement, even when our own resources are running out.
The Government has stripped Parliament of any power by asking us to pass a Bill that says the free trade agreement takes precedence over any active Canadian Parliament in case of conflict. Yet the Americans are saying that in the case of any conflict an act of the U.S. Congress will take precedence over the free trade deal. Yet this weak-kneed lackey, bootlicking Government is actually signing an agreement which states that the free trade agreement will take precedence over any act of Canadian Parliament. It is asking Members of the House to approve a deal that will bind us to future American trade law. If we violate future American trade law, not yet passed by an act of Congress, we could face a million dollar fine or go to jail.

June 29, 1988
Canada-US. Free Trade Agreement
The Conservative Government intends to ram this document through Parliament. It is restricting the rights of Members of Parliament to free speech and is limiting our opportunity to put on the record not only the faults of the deal but the hidden agenda to destroy social benefits, unemployment insurance programs, and medicare.
By hook or by crook, the Conservatives on the back-bench are going to get the kind of level playing field we know is secretly coveted by them. They cannot come forward and do it publicly. They could not cut back on senior citizens pensions publicly because people revolted. They will do it through the back door and blame it on the Americans.
The Government does not want the people of Canada to know what is in the deal. That is why it is ramming this legislation through Parliament. That is why we are not being given an opportunity in committee to fully explore it through hearings across the country. The interpretation of this agreement has not yet been passed through the U.S. Congress.
The Government wants Canadians to consider instead the great principle of free trade and whether they are for or against it. Many Canadians will say that they want to free our
trading policies and trade with the world. But they will also say that they do not want to sacrifice their Canadian way of life in the process. We do not want to give up our right to an independent foreign policy, an independent social policy. We do not want to give up the right for our children to pass laws in the Canadian Parliament that will shape the future of our generations. As a result of this document we are closing the options for future generations to develop a Canadian life style, a Canadian dream.
The Government is selling out to the Americans just so a desperate Prime Minister can have something with which to go to the polls. It will not work. He is not to be trusted. I urge the Government to call an election. They talk about Goebbels. The Government should call an election and let the people decide.
